1_revocation_reset_frame.evidence: probe1 (23/23 checks): two concurrent subscribers each received exactly one signed reset frame, reason authorization_changed, conversationId stream-reset, validated by validateEventEnvelope and Ed25519 signature verification against the pinned service key; reset was the LAST event before end (no frames after); pre-revocation frame preceded reset (ordering proof); post-revocation subscribe rejected 401 unauthorized. Bypass-hole analysis: exactly one _writeRaw call site exists (the bypass branch of _resetOne); bypass:true is passed only from dropDevice; the bypass frame content is hardcoded {conversationId: stream-reset, ownerRevision: 0, event: reset} — attacker-influenced non-reset frames cannot reach the bypass path because _writeRaw is never invoked with ordinary journal frames. dropDevice triggers only on device-inactive or null-authority (revocation, re-pair, replay-epoch loss, expiry) — never attacker-triggerable for an active device.

2_replay_continuity.evidence: probe2 (10/10): revision advancement (+5) after journaling does NOT reset; replay continues the SAME streamGeneration (genA=2, replay gens=2). Regression directions probed: backendInstance change → exactly one reset (cursor_expired, generation strictly advanced 2→6); workspaceEpoch bump → exactly one reset; cross-project transfer to another GRANTED project (cwd move) → exactly one reset. Masking analysis: the epoch-invalidation argument is sound because authorizationState() hashes per-conversation [conversationId, namespace, identity, epoch, projectId] for every granted conversation; identity embeds backendInstance/workspaceId/workspaceEpoch/conversationId; project transfer either flips projectId in the hash or (ungranted target) drops the tuple — every authority transition changes the hash, and reconcile runs before any publish delivery and at subscribe admission. Revision number never enters the authority string, so revision advancement cannot mask a real ownership change.

3_malformed_cursor_semantics.evidence: probe3 (12/12): charset-invalid cursor (embedded space) → 401 unauthorized, no stream opened, non-retryable, zero-uuid requestId; over-length (129 chars) → 401 unauthorized; charset-valid but shape-invalid (not_a_cursor_at_all) → exactly one reset cursor_expired, stream stays open; HMAC-mismatch well-formed cursor → exactly one reset cursor_expired; cross-device cursor minted for another device → exactly one reset cursor_expired, payload carries only {reason}, zero cross-device frame replay. Matches contract cursorTransitionTable (malformed = charset/pattern/length-invalid → reject; wellformedStale/foreign → reset).

4_device_inactive_vocabulary.evidence: probe45: behavioral probe forcing active()=null at the post-commit liveness re-read yields 401 with error.code unauthorized (closed vocabulary), retryable=false, authenticated requestId echoed, internal device_inactive never leaks. Structural: wireErrorCode(device_inactive) at the call site; device_inactive absent from WIRE_STATUS (pre-fix would have answered 500 internal_error with the internal code leaked). NOTE: admission→dispatch is fully synchronous so a real revocation cannot interleave in production — the check is pure defense-in-depth, and the probe exercises it by fault injection.

5_epoch_persistence.evidence: probe45: epochs persist across restart (fresh identities 1, re-encounter after restart still 1, no duplicate/re-persist); 100 first-encounters cost 176ms with 2280-byte file (one full atomic rewrite per first-encounter — bounded linear write cost, worst-case file ~150KB at 4096 entries); 4096-cap enforced exactly, newest survives, oldest evicted in insertion order. Eviction-regression analysis: epochFor only ever assigns literal 1 — no increment path exists anywhere — so an evicted identity reappearing at epoch 1 is value-neutral (the same value it always had); replay-protection impact is nil because owner epochs are never >1 through clock.epochFor (real epochs ride the embedded workspaceEpoch component of the identity).

6_immaterializable_replay.evidence: probe6 (16/16). 6a realistic path: oversized payload (9000 chars > 8KiB schema cap) fails the publish-time materialize probe — never journaled (head unchanged 2→2), exactly one reset sequence_gap delivered to live subscribers, stream STAYS OPEN, subsequent normal frame delivered. 6b whitebox journal injection (the state where a journaled frame cannot materialize at replay): replay emits exactly one reset sequence_gap then closes; reset cursor points AT head (past the dead frame); dead frame never delivered; reconnect with reset cursor resumes clean with no reset, stream open; stale-cursor retry yields exactly one reset per connection — bounded, no double-reset, no reset storm. Note: payload schemas cap text at 8KiB vs 64KiB frame budget, so production immaterializability is effectively unreachable — the reset-before-close logic is pure defense-in-depth, correct as implemented.

7_mobile_pairing_expired.evidence: probe7: server emits wire pairing_expired (401, retryable=false) for a dead pairing session — end-to-end observed. Swift structural verification: RemoteService.swift preserves wireCode==pairing_expired as code pairing_expired and the final retryable expression is retryable && code == pairing_rejected — pairing_expired can never be retryable; rate_limited (429) is also never retryable against the dead pairing session (attempts are budgeted server-side per session), consistent with the pre-existing design.

newFindings.status: PRE-EXISTING (not a round-2 regression — identical hook in 1d846458)
newFindings.title: SSE subscriptions are never reaped on client disconnect; zombies hold the 2-per-device stream slots until keepalive write failure (~15s)
newFindings.reproduction: probe7c + direct measurement: open stream (subs=1), destroy client socket, subscribers still 1 at +500ms/+3s; reaping occurred at 15.1s (the first keepalive interval). Root cause: handleSubscribe registers req.on('close') AFTER the awaits in the request pipeline, and Node fires request close at request-read completion for GET — the hook is dead code for SSE disconnects; res.on('close') is the correct signal and is never registered. In probe3e a legitimately-signed fresh subscribe was answered 503 server_busy solely because two client-closed streams were still zombies.
newFindings.impact: availability-only: a mobile client that disconnects/reconnects twice within ~15s (normal on network flaps or app backgrounding) gets transient 503 server_busy; self-heals at the next keepalive failure; retryable=true on the wire so contract-conformant clients recover. No security or data-integrity impact.
newFindings.recommendation: register res.on('close') (or res.socket.once('close')) instead of/in addition to req.on('close'); add a contract test that destroys a subscriber and asserts prompt reaping + resubscribe capacity.

newFindings.title: mobile sandbox treats charset-valid-but-shape-invalid cursors as malformed (reject unauthorized); desktop treats them as wellformedStale/foreign (exactly one reset cursor_expired)
newFindings.reproduction: src/remote/sandbox.ts decodeCursor: any cursor failing the strict g<n>_s<n>_<tag> shape returns malformed → unauthorized (line 860), whereas desktop handleSubscribe resets (probe3c confirmed reset). Contract cursorPattern (^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,128}$) makes only charset/length the malformed grammar, so desktop is contract-correct and the sandbox diverges.
newFindings.impact: test-fidelity only: sandbox serves no production traffic and clients never construct cursors (contract cursorDelivery.format); but sandbox-driven client tests cannot exercise the reset-rebuild path for shape-invalid cursors, and m5-deferred-items.md does not record the divergence.
newFindings.recommendation: record in docs/acceptance/m5-deferred-items.md or align sandbox decodeCursor with desktop semantics.

newFindings.title: epoch persistence mechanism cannot deliver its stated replay-protection purpose: epochFor never increments — every identity's epoch is always literal 1
newFindings.reproduction: probe45-structural: epochFor assigns only the map lookup and literal 1; no bump path exists anywhere in adapters.mjs; therefore the eviction regression (reappearing identity → 1) is value-neutral and restart persistence protects nothing that memory did not already. Real replay protection rides the workspaceEpoch embedded in the identity string (and device replayEpoch), both unaffected.
newFindings.impact: none on security or correctness; cosmetic/measurement debt — the persisted epochs map grows and rewrites on every first-encounter (measured 176ms/100 identities, file ~2.3KB at 100 entries, worst-case ~150KB at the 4096 cap) for zero protective effect.
newFindings.recommendation: either implement actual epoch bumping on authority re-encounter (if intended) or drop the persistence and document that workspaceEpoch carries epoch semantics; in neither case is this a blocker for round-2 acceptance.
